material: Woodcut on laid paper
provenance: Colnaghi & Co., London, their stock number 'C.11355' pencil in verso | | Albrecht Dürer's unprecedented technical mastery of woodcuts changed the history of printmaking. He was incredibly ahead of his time in his ability to achieve expressive depth and detail in his compositions that have captivated viewers over the course of centuries. Samson Rending the Lion is a signature example of Dürer's early woodcuts from the 1490s, brimming with virtuosic, sinuous lines. Dürer captures a spectacular graduation of tone by ingeniously carving bolder, flatter lines of the image closer to the surface of the block while other areas with more detailed, pointed lines lie deeper in the block, on a slightly lower plane. This creates a highly dynamic composition, full of contrast and explosive detail as Dürer depicts one of the most famous tales of the Old Testament. | | Samson, the last Old Testament judge, is acclaimed for his superhuman strength, renown for being powerful enough to have ripped apart a lion with his bare hands. As Samson stomps on the lion's neck and brazenly grips the lion's jaw, Dürer symbolically showcases the historic battle between Christ and the Devil, good and evil. Dürer enhances this theme of light and dark, by purposely leaving certain sections of the sky and water blank letting the paper shine through to contrast his bold linework. No detail is left out, for example, in the cluster of foliage atop the hillside, Dürer carefully makes each tree visually different from the next as every branch is carved with intention. From each meandering, curl in Samson's locks, the billowing lines of the lion's mane, to the jagged leaves of the nettle in the lower left corner, every element of this illustrious woodcut is executed with intentional purpose. | | While woodblocks are immensely hard to cut, over time they can degrade and crack under the immense pressure of numerous, later printings. Therefore, this early impression is rare opportunity to study Dürer's woodcuts with the depth and detail that he intended, before the superb contrast diminished over time.

artwork_title: Portrait de Jacqueline au Chapeau de Paille (Tête de Femme)
material: Linocut in colors on Arches paper
provenance: Acquired directly from the publisher by the present owner |  | This exceptional linocut portrays Jacqueline Roque (1927 - 1986), Picasso's second wife and final muse. Picasso obsessively created images of Jacqueline, enraptured by her large almond-shaped eyes, bold brows and elegant profile. The couple married in Vallauris in March of 1961, after meeting years prior while Jacqueline worked at Madoura Pottery. Picasso was enthralled with perfecting this portrait of his new wife, as he created several different versions in January of 1962. Even in the middle of winter, Picasso was drawn to a springtime color palette carving red and green figural lines, topped with a yellow straw hat. The bright colors are an ode to the joy and rebirth Picasso felt marrying Jacqueline just two weeks before the spring equinox.

material: aquatint on Arches paper
provenance: Marina Picasso (Lugt 3698) | Frederick Mulder, London | Private Collection of Catherine Woodard & Nelson Blitz, Jr. | Sotheby's, New York, Important Prints & Multiples, Lot 96, 23 October 2017 | Acquired directly from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Williamstown, Massachusetts, The Clark Art Institute, Picasso: Encounters, 2017 | | This monumental portrait of Françoise Gilot (1921 - 2023) titled La Femme à la Fenêtre from 1952, is one of Pablo Picasso's largest prints done entirely in aquatint. Picasso implemented the sugar-lift aquatint technique, a method he almost single-handedly developed, which allowed him to brush the image directly onto the printing plate to achieve a painterly effect while capturing a stunning variation in tone. The present impression is particularly remarkable as it exudes dramatic contrasts and exquisite tonal depth throughout the composition. | | Picasso first encountered Gilot in the Spring of 1943 at Le Catalan, a Left Bank restaurant near his studio on Rue des Grands-Augustins. He was immediately drawn to Gilot, even though at the time he was still with his lover, the French photographer and painter, Dora Maar. In 1946 however, Picasso and Gilot quickly moved in together had two children, Claude and Paloma. Gilot became a beloved, longtime muse featured in many of Picasso's painted, printed and ceramic bodies of work. Picasso's depictions of Gilot echoed the feelings of their relationship. In the beginning, Gilot's portraits had an inviting warmth, but in La Femme à la Fenêtre, about a decade after their first meeting, Gilot has a somber expression and appears to be almost trapped within the frame. In 1953, only a year after the completion of this famous print, Françoise split from Picasso. The work captures Gilot's longing to escape at the end of their partnership as she gazes away from the viewer, her hands pressed against the windowpane. | | Picasso masterfully documents the intense feelings in his relationship while showcasing his virtuosity as a printmaker, using aquatint to create rich depth and accentuate the mood in the portrait. The present work is an early, rare impression, one of only four executed before steel-facing on this paper. The process of steel-facing involves coating the copper printing plate in steel in order to preserve its durability. While this increases the longevity of the copper plate, it can diminish the tonal depth and textural quality of a print. As this example is one of the very few before steel-facing, it allows viewers the rare opportunity to study Picasso's intended effect of aquatint in its truest form.

material: Polystone, acrylic, colored pencil, mixed media
provenance: Private Collection, Massachusetts | | Yoshitomo Nara is a contemporary artist whose work across media has captured the world by storm. Drawing upon a range of influences, from popular culture to anime and punk rock, Nara pushes boundaries with a seemingly simplistic approach by personifying the cultural phenomenon of kawaii that emphasizes cuteness through an embrace of childlike innocence and imagination. His recurring childlike characters that include big-headed girls, sleepless figures, and playful animals are multifaceted; dig beneath the veneer and the playful appearance recedes to embody a wealth of emotion from vulnerability and loneliness to menacing rebellion. | | For Hand Searching, Nara utilizes his popular big-headed girl motif and depicts her with a subdued smirk and wide eyes with a skewed gaze that neither confronts the viewer, nor allows them in. The sculpture here is a three-dimensional representation that Nara explored in a 2004 colored pencil drawing of the same scene. In both works, the figure appears to be far more mature than her youthful appearance lets on. Presented with neither hands nor feet, but an oversized shirt, the viewer is invited to ask where exactly the searching hand has gone. | | Perched atop a desolate island with an untrustworthy stare, it is the figure's baby-blue shirt that opens a door towards resilience. Drawing comparisons to the animated characters that preceded her, the blue shirt is referential to the empowered female figures that populate many of the films that feature strong-willed heroines. From Cinderella and Belle to Alice and Elsa, these protagonists in one way or another found themselves on their own metaphorical islands that required strength and adaptability to persevere, a connection shared with Nara's own heroine.
